newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts see sluggish fine paper prices.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see sluggish fine paper prices.

text.p: The combination of high pulp inventories and new capacity was likely to keep a lid on fine paper prices in the short term, analysts said on Thursday.

"Fine paper producers announced price hikes from the start of the New Year and that means wholesalers have built up inventories ahead of the year-end," an analyst working for a British subcontractor in the paper sector told Reuters.
He was sceptical about the success of the price rise that took effect from January 1.
"I hope, naturally, that it will go through, but there is a clear risk that it won't," he said.

"There has been an inventory build-up at wholesalers and you cannot sell the same paper twice," he said, referring to increased North America and Scandinavia (NorScan) pulp stocks and expectations about new capacity.

Swedish forestry group Stora AB estimates that from 1997 to 1999, there will be additional capacity of about two million tonnes in uncoated fine paper and about 3.5 million tonnes in coated fine paper.

But if manufacturers can limit their capacity utilisation, it would be possible to keep fine paper prices stable during 1997, Lars Hadder, chief analyst at Stora Fine Paper, said at a forestry seminar in Stockholm on Thursday.
"The pressure on prices probably comes from the output side, rather than from the demand side," Hadder said.
"New machines that started up last year will be up to speed this year. We must learn to use lower capacity for several years - 1997, 1998 and the beginning of 1999."
Hadder, however, admitted that such discipline was hard to achieve.
"I think that with future restructuring in Europe (with fewer manufacturers) we have good opportunities for good discipline among European manufacturers," he said.
"But in China and the rest of Asia, people think a bit differently. It will be tough."
"I find it hard to believe in such discipline. They have not succeeded with it during my twenty years in the business," the British analyst said.
A Swedish equities analyst was just as critical.
"It has never worked before, so why would it work now," he said.
